summary: An NRDC guide by Lora Shinn, published June 1, 2022 (originally June 15, 2018), explaining renewable energy and the clean-energy transition. It covers what renewable energy is, why nonrenewable 'dirty' fossil fuels are harmful, and the main types: solar, wind, hydroelectric, biomass, geothermal and ocean energy. It notes that some sources marketed as renewable, such as biomass and large dams, involve serious trade-offs, and closes with home options like rooftop solar, geothermal heat pumps, small wind turbines, net metering and buying renewable certificates.
one_line: NRDC guide explaining renewable energy types, their environmental trade-offs, and home options such as solar, geothermal heat pumps and net metering.
key_facts: Renewable energy comes from natural sources or processes that are constantly replenished, such as sunlight and wind.
The note states that renewables account for more than 12 percent of U.S. energy generation.
According to the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, more energy from the sun falls on the earth in one hour than is used by everyone in the world in one year.
Solar supplies nearly 3 percent of U.S. electricity generation, and 46 percent of all new generating capacity came from solar in 2021.
Wind accounts for 9.2 percent of U.S. electricity generation.
Top wind power states include California, Iowa, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas.
Hydropower is the largest renewable energy source for electricity in the United States, though wind energy is soon expected to take over the lead.
Small hydroelectric plants with installed capacity below about 40 megawatts do not tend to cause as much environmental damage, as they divert only a fraction of the flow.
Biomass is often mistakenly described as a clean, renewable fuel, and recent science shows many forms of biomass, especially from forests, produce higher carbon emissions than fossil fuels.
Sawdust and chips from sawmills that would otherwise quickly decompose and release carbon can be a low-carbon energy source.
Geothermal plants typically have low emissions if they pump the steam and water they use back into the reservoir.
Geothermal systems can be initially expensive to install but typically pay off within 5 to 10 years.
Net metering allows homeowners to pay only the difference between the grid-supplied electricity consumed and what they have produced.
Tidal barrages work much like dams and are located in an ocean bay or lagoon, and some tidal energy approaches may harm wildlife.
Renewable energy certificates can be purchased to offset electricity use if renewable energy is not available through a utility.
